articles.label: Public Records
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1 million legal bill: What 18 months of outside counsel bought taxpayers
articles.dek: A Flightline review of invoices and contracts reveals which fights the county chose to pay for — and which ones it's still losing.
brief: Escambia County paid $2.1 million to outside law firms between January 2025 and June 2026, according to invoices obtained through public records requests.
Three ongoing lawsuits account for more than half of total spending, including the Beulah interchange condemnation and a whistleblower case filed by a former Public Works employee.
The county attorney's office declined to provide cost projections for pending litigation, citing attorney-client privilege.
articles.body:
The invoice arrived at the Escambia County Administrator's office on a Tuesday in March. Thirty-seven pages. $127,450 for February's work alone.

It came from Allen Norton & Blue, a Pensacola firm handling one of the county's three active federal lawsuits. The billing entries read like a novel written in six-minute increments: 0.3 hours for an email review, 1.2 hours for a phone conference, 4.5 hours for deposition preparation.

This is how Escambia County spent $2.1 million on outside legal counsel over the past 18 months.

The Flightline obtained 847 pages of invoices, engagement letters and payment records through a public records request filed in April. The documents cover January 2025 through June 2026 and represent every payment the county made to private law firms — work that fell outside the scope of the county attorney's office.

The picture that emerges is one of a county government fighting battles on multiple fronts, some of its own making.

Where the money went

Three matters consumed 58 percent of total outside counsel spending.

The largest: $614,000 to GrayRobinson for condemnation proceedings related to the Beulah interchange project. The county is seeking to acquire 23 parcels through eminent domain to complete the I-10 connector. Fourteen property owners are contesting the county's valuation offers.

Second: $412,000 to Allen Norton & Blue for defense of Richardson v. Escambia County, a whistleblower retaliation suit filed in the Northern District of Florida. Marcus Richardson, a former Public Works supervisor, alleges he was terminated in 2024 after reporting safety violations at the Central Landfill. The case is set for trial in October.

Third: $189,000 to Carlton Fields for representation in an ongoing dispute with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection over stormwater permit compliance at the Perdido Landfill. The county is appealing $340,000 in fines.

The remaining $885,000 was spread across 14 different matters, including contract disputes with construction firms, personnel grievances and specialized bond counsel work.

Hourly rates and staffing

Billing rates varied widely. Senior partners at GrayRobinson billed at $475 per hour. Associates at smaller firms charged $225. Paralegals ranged from $95 to $150.

Some invoices showed as many as seven attorneys billing time on the same matter in a single month. The Richardson case, for instance, listed four attorneys, a paralegal and a litigation support specialist on February's invoice alone.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh raised questions about attorney staffing at a May budget workshop.

"I'm not a lawyer," Bergosh said. "But I've got to ask — do we need five people in a room for a deposition?"

County Attorney Alison Rogers said outside counsel decisions are made based on case complexity and risk exposure. She declined to second-guess specific staffing choices.

"We engage firms with expertise the county attorney's office doesn't have in-house," Rogers said in a written response to Flightline questions. "The alternative would be hiring specialists as county employees, which carries its own costs."

What the county won't say

The Flightline requested projected total costs for the three largest ongoing matters. Rogers declined, citing attorney-client privilege and work product protections.

"Disclosing litigation strategy or cost projections could prejudice the county's position," Rogers wrote.

The county also declined to provide any internal assessments of likely outcomes in pending cases.

This much is knowable from public court records: The Richardson whistleblower case survived a motion to dismiss in December 2025. The judge, in denying the county's motion, wrote that Richardson had presented "sufficient factual allegations to proceed to discovery." That's not a ruling on the merits. But it means the county couldn't end the case early and cheaply.

The Beulah condemnation cases have produced mixed results. The county prevailed in three early settlements at or near its appraised values. But two property owners have obtained independent appraisals valuing their land at more than double the county's offers. Those cases are headed to jury trials.

How this compares

The $2.1 million figure represents a 34 percent increase over the previous 18-month period, when the county spent $1.57 million on outside counsel.

Much of the increase traces to the Beulah interchange project, which began generating significant legal costs in mid-2025 when negotiations with property owners stalled.

County Administrator Wes Moreno said the infrastructure project's legal costs were anticipated.

"You don't build a $78 million interchange without some property disputes," Moreno said at a June commission meeting. "That's the cost of progress."

Commissioner Lumon May asked whether the county had budgeted adequately for legal contingencies. Moreno said the project included a 10 percent contingency fund, portions of which have been allocated to legal costs.

The Richardson case was not anticipated. The termination occurred in August 2024. The lawsuit followed three months later.

Oversight questions

Outside counsel contracts do not require individual commissioner approval. The county administrator has authority to engage firms for matters under $50,000. Larger engagements require only county attorney sign-off.

Commissioners receive quarterly reports summarizing outside counsel expenditures by matter. The reports do not include copies of invoices or detailed billing entries.

Commissioner May said in an interview that he has requested more granular reporting.

"Two million dollars is real money," May said. "The public has a right to know what it's buying. I'd like to see us post these invoices online, same as we do with other expenditures."

Rogers said her office is reviewing whether redacted invoices could be posted without compromising privileged information. She offered no timeline.

The next quarterly outside counsel report is scheduled for the August 3 commission meeting.

articles.label: Downtown
articles.headline: The Palafox parking problem nobody wants to solve
articles.dek: Three proposed garages. Two failed votes. One city council that keeps punting. Meanwhile, downtown business owners watch summer crowds circle the block.
brief: Pensacola City Council has rejected two parking garage proposals since 2024, with a third now stalled in committee
Downtown business owners report losing customers who give up after circling blocks during peak hours
The city's last parking study, conducted in 2019, counted 847 fewer public spaces than projected demand
articles.body:
Saturday night on Palafox Street. The temperature has dropped to something tolerable, and the sidewalks are thick with people drifting between restaurants and bars. At the corner of Palafox and Romana, a silver Honda Accord rolls past for the third time in ten minutes. The driver cranes her neck toward a loading zone, then keeps moving.

This is the scene downtown business owners describe when they talk about parking. Not empty lots. Not a city without visitors. The opposite problem: people who want to come but can't find a place to put their cars.

"I watch it happen from my window," said Marcus Chen, owner of Gulf Standard Supply on South Palafox. "Somebody circles, circles again, and then they just leave. I've had customers text me that they gave up."

The city has known about this for years. In 2019, a parking utilization study commissioned by the Downtown Improvement Board found that weekend evenings pushed public lot occupancy above 95 percent. The study projected a shortfall of 847 spaces by 2025, assuming moderate growth. Downtown has grown faster than moderate.

Three times since then, proposals for structured parking have come before Pensacola City Council. Three times, the proposals have stalled or died.

The proposals that weren't

The first serious attempt came in late 2024. A public-private partnership would have built a 400-space garage on the city-owned lot at Jefferson and Baylen streets. The developer, Coastal Urban Partners, proposed funding 60 percent of construction costs in exchange for ground-floor retail rights and a 30-year revenue-sharing agreement.

Pensacola City Council member Delores Patterson raised concerns about the revenue split. "We're giving away a public asset for pennies," she said at the November 2024 meeting. The vote failed 4-3.

Six months later, a modified version returned. Same location, adjusted terms: 70 percent developer funding, 25-year agreement, city retains ground-floor control. This time Pensacola City Council member Robert Alston objected to the design, calling the proposed six-story structure "out of scale with the historic district." The vote failed again, 4-3, with different members on each side.

The third proposal arrived this spring. The Downtown Improvement Board pitched a city-funded garage on the Palafox and Main lot, with bonds repaid through parking revenue. No private developer. No retail component. Just parking.

It never reached a vote. The proposal has been sitting in the Community Redevelopment Committee since April. Pensacola City Council President Angela Morrison said the committee is "still reviewing financial projections." She declined to provide a timeline for when it might move forward.

What the numbers say

The city's parking inventory downtown includes approximately 1,200 public spaces in surface lots and on-street metered spots. Private lots add another 800, most restricted to business patrons or monthly renters.

The 2019 study projected demand of roughly 2,850 spaces during peak periods by 2025. Updated figures aren't available—the city hasn't commissioned a new study—but the Downtown Improvement Board's informal counts suggest the projection was conservative.

On a Saturday in June, board staff counted 94 percent occupancy across public lots by 7 p.m. On-street spaces hit 100 percent by 6:15 p.m. The adjacent residential streets in the East Hill neighborhood were lined with cars displaying temporary parking passes from downtown restaurants.

"We're exporting our parking problem into the neighborhoods," said Jennifer Walsh, executive director of the Downtown Improvement Board. "That creates its own set of conflicts."

The business owners

Chen has operated Gulf Standard Supply for eight years. He sells vintage furniture, home goods, and local art. Weekend afternoons are his busiest time. They're also when parking is worst.

"I've started telling people to come Thursday or Friday if they can," he said. "Saturday, I lose sales. I know I do. I just can't tell you exactly how many."

Three blocks north, Rachel Drummond runs Emerald Coast Coffee. She said the parking crunch hits hardest during Gallery Night and other downtown events.

"Those are supposed to be our biggest nights," Drummond said. "But if somebody's coming from East Hill or Cordova Park, they need to leave their house 45 minutes early just to find a spot. Some people just don't bother anymore."

Not every business owner supports new garages. Tom Whitfield, who owns a law firm on Palafox, argued that the parking problem is overstated.

"There's always a spot if you're willing to walk a few blocks," Whitfield said. "People want valet service. That's not what downtown is."

Whitfield added that he worries a large garage would change the neighborhood's character. "You put up a parking structure, you're admitting you've become a certain kind of place," he said. "I'm not sure that's what we want."

The council's silence

The Flightline requested interviews with all seven Pensacola City Council members. Two agreed to speak on background. None would discuss the parking issue on the record.

The reluctance is notable. Council members have been vocal about other downtown issues—short-term rental regulations, noise ordinances, sidewalk maintenance. Parking prompts a different response.

One council member, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the issue is politically toxic.

"Nobody wants to vote for something that costs money and might not work," the member said. "And nobody wants to vote against parking and then get blamed when it's still a mess five years from now. So we just don't vote."

The result is paralysis. Each proposal gets picked apart for different reasons. Financial terms. Architectural design. Location. The objections shift, but the outcome stays the same.

What happens next

The Downtown Improvement Board's proposal remains in committee. Walsh said she's been asked to provide additional financial modeling showing how different usage scenarios would affect bond repayment. She hopes to have that ready by September.

"We'll try again," she said. "That's all we can do."

Meanwhile, the Honda Accord eventually finds a spot. It's four blocks away, on a residential street in the Seville Historic District. The driver walks toward Palafox in sandals not designed for that distance.

Somewhere, a business owner is watching the door, waiting to see if she makes it.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week arrives with new flight patterns — and new noise complaints
articles.dek: Residents near the base say low-altitude practice runs have intensified. The Navy says nothing has changed. GPS flight data suggests otherwise.
brief: Homecoming air show scheduled for July 18-19 at NAS Pensacola
Flight tracking data shows practice runs extending further west over residential areas than in previous years
Navy public affairs maintains all flight operations fall within established parameters
articles.body:
The F/A-18 Super Hornet banked hard over Summit Boulevard at 2:47 p.m. Tuesday, close enough that Maria Gonzalez could see the pilot's helmet through her kitchen window. Her coffee mug rattled off the counter. The dog bolted under the bed. Her three-year-old started screaming.

"This is not normal," Gonzalez said. "I've lived here nine years. I know what normal sounds like."

She's not alone. Since practice runs intensified last week ahead of the July 18-19 homecoming air show at NAS Pensacola, the base's public affairs office has fielded 43 noise complaints from residents in the Warrington and Brownsville neighborhoods — triple the number logged during the same pre-show period in 2025, according to records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

The Navy's official position: nothing has changed.

"Blue Angels flight demonstrations and practice schedules operate within long-established parameters approved by Naval Air Forces," said Lt. Cmdr. Jessica Walters, a spokesperson for NAS Pensacola. "We appreciate our neighbors' patience as we prepare to showcase naval aviation excellence."

The data tells a different story

Flight tracking data compiled by ADS-B Exchange, a publicly accessible aircraft tracking network, shows a measurable shift in the team's practice patterns this season. The Flightline analyzed 127 individual flight tracks from Blue Angels practices conducted between July 1 and July 12.

The westernmost point of the standard diamond formation pass has moved approximately 0.4 nautical miles further into residential airspace compared to the same period in 2024 and 2025. Minimum altitudes during the "low transition" maneuver — the crowd-favorite moment when jets scream past at near-rooftop level — have dropped from an average of 387 feet above ground level to 312 feet.

That 75-foot difference translates to roughly a 40% increase in perceived sound intensity on the ground, according to Dr. Kenneth Rashid, an acoustics researcher at the University of West Florida who reviewed the data at The Flightline's request.

"Sound pressure doesn't scale linearly with distance," Rashid said. "When you're talking about supersonic aircraft at low altitude, every foot matters. A lot."

'We bought the house knowing'

Not everyone in the affected neighborhoods is complaining. At the Vet's Memorial dog park on Fairfield Drive, opinions split roughly down the middle on a recent Thursday afternoon.

"We bought the house knowing this was Blue Angels country," said Robert Tanner, 67, a retired Marine who moved to Warrington from Jacksonville in 2019. "People who complain about jet noise next to a naval air station are like people who buy a house next to a hog farm and complain about the smell."

But longtime residents say there's a difference between accepting occasional noise and experiencing what they describe as a sustained assault.

"I'm not anti-military. My father was Navy," said Patricia Webb, who has lived on Muldoon Road since 1987. "But something's different this year. The windows shake. The pictures fall off the wall. My husband has PTSD from Vietnam and he can't be in the house during practice anymore."

Webb said she's called the base complaint line four times in the past week. Each time, she said, she was told her concerns would be "logged and forwarded." She has received no follow-up.

Why the shift?

The Navy declined to make anyone from the Blue Angels demonstration team available for an interview. In a written statement, the team said its 2026 show routine "incorporates minor adjustments to maximize the spectator experience while maintaining all safety margins."

Aviation analysts who spoke with The Flightline offered several possible explanations for the changed flight patterns.

The team transitioned from the legacy F/A-18 Hornet to the larger, more powerful F/A-18 Super Hornet in 2021. While the aircraft has been in service for five years now, teams continue to refine maneuvers as pilots gain experience with the platform's different handling characteristics.

Additionally, construction of a new hangar complex on the southeast corner of the airfield, completed in March, may have prompted controllers to shift certain approach and departure corridors.

"When you change the geometry of the ground infrastructure, you often have to adjust the geometry of the air operations," said Marcus Chen, a former naval aviator and current aviation consultant based in Mobile. "It's possible they pushed some patterns west to accommodate the new construction without really thinking through the noise implications for the residential areas."

What happens next

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes the affected neighborhoods, said he's been in contact with base leadership about the complaints.

"I've expressed the concerns of my constituents," Bergosh said in a phone interview Friday. "The base has been receptive to hearing us out. Whether that translates into any actual changes remains to be seen."

Bergosh noted that the county has limited leverage over military flight operations, which fall under federal jurisdiction. Short of a congressional intervention, residents have few formal avenues for redress.

The homecoming air show itself is expected to draw more than 150,000 spectators to NAS Pensacola over the two-day event. Practice runs will continue daily through Thursday, weather permitting, with sessions typically running from 11:30 a.m. to noon and again from 2:30 p.m. to 3 p.m.

For Maria Gonzalez, that means five more days of rattling windows and a terrified toddler.

"I love this city," she said. "I love the Blue Angels. I understand they need to practice. I just want someone to acknowledge that what they're doing this year is different, and maybe talk to us about it instead of pretending everything's the same."

She paused as another jet thundered overhead, heading east toward the base.

"That's all. Just talk to us."
